source: Beger, Yi, Fu, Denton, Moskvichev, Tsai, Rajamanickam, Mitchell (2026) Distinguishing Performance From Competence in Evaluations of Humanlike Abstract Reasoning (NeurIPS 2026 E&D, v5)
finding: Gap 1. Reasoning models (o3, o4-mini, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro) reach or pass human output accuracy on text ConceptARC, but a large share of their correct answers rest on less abstract rules than the test designers intended.
numbers: 480 ConceptARC tasks. Human pass@1 grid accuracy 73%. o3 text medium effort no tools 77.1%, with tools 75.6%. o4-mini medium+tools 77.7%. Claude Sonnet 4 60.2% (72.5% after re-scoring bad formats), Gemini 2.5 Pro 66.0%, GPT-4o 14.6%. About 27% of o3 and Gemini correct outputs (19% Claude) had correct-unintended or incorrect rules versus about 7% of human correct outputs. Four annotators, 192 rules, mean agreement 84.8%, kappa 0.70.
quote: accuracy alone can substantially overestimate AI competence in textual modalities while underestimating it in visual modalities
limits: Human rules were missing for 19% of correct outputs and not collected for wrong outputs, so the comparison is only on correct answers. Single benchmark. Newer models not evaluated. Rule coding needs judgement.
agent_relevance: Accuracy on analogy puzzles overstates abstraction in 2025 reasoning models. The scaffold should check the stated rule against intended relational concepts, not only the answer. Treat a correct answer with a spurious rule as a risk signal.

source: Beger et al. (2026) ConceptARC, effort and tool ablations (same paper, appendix tables 3, 7 and Section 5)
finding: Gap 1, tool-use part. Python tools do not lift text accuracy; more reasoning effort does. In the visual modality tools help and effort alone does not. So the text-side pass is not explained by code execution.
numbers: o3 text: low effort 68.3%, medium 77.1%, low+tools 67.9%, medium+tools 75.6%. o3 visual: low 6.5%, medium 5.6%, low+tools 18.2%, medium+tools 29.2%. Visual rule check: correct-intended rules 40.0% vs correct grids 29.2% (o3), 14.4% vs 6.9% (Claude), 23.5% vs 5.8% (Gemini). Re-run on 48 cases three times: rule-label consistency 66.0% to 70.9% between runs.
limits: Only o3 got the full effort x tool grid. pass@1, one prompt family (the ARC Prize o3 prompt). The paper says other prompts may do better.
agent_relevance: For text relational tasks, thinking tokens buy more than code tools. For perception-heavy inputs, tools matter. Budget the scaffold for reasoning and keep tools for re-encoding or checking.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024, arXiv v1 2411.14215) Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Gap 7. Full-length study of the Webb tasks with variants. Humans stay high on counterfactual letter-string variants while GPT models fall. For story analogies GPT-4 shows a strong answer-order effect and some paraphrase sensitivity.
numbers: Story analogies: GPT-4 accuracy 89% (16/18) when Story A was correct but 61% (11/18) when Story B was correct. Letter strings: human accuracy higher than every GPT model in every cell, much higher for zero-generalisation problems. Human sample per cell 92 to 384. Error types (Table 8): GPT-4 used an alternate rule in 38.59% of errors, GPT-3 in 5.81%; incorrect rule applied in over 30% of GPT errors vs about 15% for humans.
limits: I read the abstract, sample sizes, order-effect text and error table; I did not extract every Table 1 cell. GPT-3, 3.5, 4 only (no reasoning models). Humans not tested on 2 and 3 generalisations with symbol alphabets.
agent_relevance: Cheap invariance tests for the scaffold: swap answer order, paraphrase the source, permute the alphabet. A drop under these means the answer came from a shortcut.

source: Hellwig, Zuidema, Stevenson, Lewis (2026) Transformer See, Transformer Do: Copying as an Intermediate Step in Learning Analogical Reasoning (COLM 2026)
finding: Gap 1 and 9. Small 3-layer transformers trained by meta-learning on letter-string analogies match frontier LLMs, but only when copy tasks are in the training mix. Copy tasks create matching heads between example input and output pairs (an induction-like binding step). Generalisation to new alphabets needs many training alphabets. Entirely new transformations are not learned.
numbers: Best run (200 permuted alphabets + copy tasks): 96.7% on seen alphabets with seen transformations, 93.9% on new alphabets with seen transformations; new transformations only 13.1% and 12.3%. With 20 alphabets and no copy: 60.9% and 26.5%. Matching heads appeared in 100% of runs with copy tasks and about 25% without. Frontier models compared: GPT 5.2, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-OSS 120B, Llama 70B and 17B, GPT 4.1.
limits: Per-frontier-model numbers were in a figure and could not be read from the text; I only have the paper's statement that the best run is on par with them and beats most on compositional transformations. Closed synthetic task. Interpretability shown for one task.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a relational-binding step as a learned mechanism (like LISA role binding). Failure on new transformations says a fixed rule library does not cover novel relations; the scaffold must induce rules per problem.

source: Chen, Wang, Wang (2026) ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning (v3, Oct 2026)
finding: Gap 1. A far-analogy benchmark (real-world concept to grid transformation) with 200 tasks and a human study. Frontier 2025-26 models stay below humans; Claude Opus 4.5 is far lower than GPT 5.2.
numbers: Human pass@1 average 68.96% (58.35% strict), humans on tasks solved by 2 or more people 93.5% to 96%. LLM pass@3 union over 12 attempts: GPT 5.2 51.20% (48.33% strict), Gemini 3 Pro 43.06% (29.19%), Grok 4.1 Fast 24.88% (18.66%), Claude Opus 4.5 8.61% (7.18%). Paired bootstrap on 200 tasks: strongest model 10.13 points below humans strict, 17.67 typo-tolerant; Claude Opus 4.5 51.63 below. Reasoning effort left at model default via OpenRouter.
limits: LLMs got pass@3 across 4 prompt setups while humans got pass@1, so the gap is if anything understated. Table text in the PDF is partly scrambled (columns for CoT language vs CoT+analogical VL could not be assigned to models with certainty). Claude result may reflect output-format failures; the paper does not separate those.
agent_relevance: Far analogy with real-world source and abstract target is still open for the best models. Use this family to test the mapping step, not letter strings.

source: Chen et al. (2026) ARCANA, ConceptSIR section 6-7 (Copycat-inspired LLM pipeline)
finding: Gap 5. The first LLM pipeline I found built on Copycat ideas: propose concepts, slip concepts (re-describe), introspect, execute as code, reflect, loop. The LLM is treated as an implicit Slipnet. It solves some tasks that direct prompting does not, but the evidence is small and the authors say it is not a general framework.
numbers: Subset of 17 tasks chosen for low direct-LLM accuracy (from 11 categories). Strict exact match, one run, up to 5 loops: 9/17 solved across 7 categories, 2.22 loops on average for solved cases. Gemini 3 Pro for proposal, slippage, introspection; GPT 5.2 for code. No baseline on the same 17 tasks and no equal-token comparison in the quantitative section.
limits: Subset picked for difficulty, no control arm, no confidence interval, one run per task. Needs code execution and prediction-error-dependent mutation, so the authors say it is not general.
agent_relevance: Direction to copy: loop of describe, map, test by execution, re-describe on error. Not proof that interleaved re-representation beats a fixed description; that test is still missing.

source: Chen et al. (2026) ARCANA, analogy-correctness analysis
finding: Gap 2 (partial). When the model is prompted to produce an explicit analogy target first, correct analogies co-occur with correct answers, so the analogy step is a bottleneck. This is correlation within a prompt condition, not explicit mapping versus free chain of thought at equal tokens.
numbers: Pulley category: Gemini 3 Pro analogy correctness 100% and answer accuracy 67%; GPT 5.2 analogy correctness 0% and answer accuracy 0%. The analogical-prompt arm used vision input (CoT+Ana VL), the CoT arm was language-only, so arms differ in modality as well as prompt.
limits: Confounded: modality and prompt differ between arms. Pass@3 and manual scoring. No ACME-style scoring of candidate correspondences.
agent_relevance: Supports making the source-to-target analogy an explicit, checkable intermediate object. Does not show it beats free CoT.

source: Puranam, Sen, Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs Help Improve Analogical Reasoning For Strategic Decisions? Experimental Evidence from Humans and GPT-4
finding: Gap 4. Separates retrieval from matching. With a hint to use an earlier story, GPT-4 always uses the correct source (recall 1.00) but also applies the wrong source about half the time (precision about 0.5). Without a hint, the AI runs never used the correct analogy. Humans are conservative: high precision, low recall.
numbers: Humans n=199, AI n=60 runs. With hint, AI: Radiation story TP 15, FN 0, FP 14, TN 1 (precision 0.52, recall 1.00, F1 0.68); Dolphin story TP 15, FP 15 (precision 0.50, F1 0.67). Humans with hint: precision 0.67 and 0.75, recall 0.26 and 0.39. No hint: AI precision and recall 0 for both; humans recall 0.06 (Radiation) and 0.22 (Dolphin), precision 0.42 and 1.00. Authors attribute AI errors to surface-feature similarity.
limits: One GPT-4 setup, two source problems, both candidate stories shown together. Table text partly scrambled in the PDF; the numbers above agree with the prose. Management-science preprint.
agent_relevance: Matches the Ross-type dissociation: surface cues let the model retrieve and apply a wrong analog. A separate structure-based match check before transfer is justified; the model alone does not provide it.

source: Qin, Xia, Wang et al. (2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning? (v3)
finding: Gap 8. Test of Yasunaga's self-generated analogs. On math, self-generated irrelevant examples do as well or better than relevant ones; example accuracy, not relevance, drives the gain. On BIG-Bench Hard subsets relevance does help.
numbers: GPT-3.5, 500 test items per math set, 3 seeds. GSM8K+MATH average: relevant 52.4, N/A 55.8, random same-domain 55.7, random different 55.2, random biology 54.9. BBH five-task average: relevant 63.2, N/A 61.9, random-same 60.4, random-different 56.4 (row labels in the scan are shifted, so which random row gets 60.4 vs 56.4 is uncertain). Cosine relevance 0.54/0.41 (relevant) vs 0.06/0.11 (biology). Accuracy of generated examples on MATH (50 checked): relevant 62%, N/A 72%, random-same 86%.
limits: GPT-3.5 (GPT-4o-mini repeated in appendix, not read). Math only for the central claim. Example accuracy checked on 50 items per type.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that self-generated analogs help because they are analogous. Verify the example, or use a fixed verified set. Small models would produce less accurate examples.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random, fixed verified examples and cost
finding: Gap 8, cost part. Two fixed example sets generated once (ICLmath, ICLbio) after checking accuracy beat per-query self-generated relevant examples and cut inference cost, since examples are not regenerated per query. A calibration variant with accurate GPT-4 answers beat plain in-context learning on both datasets; random answers were always worst.
numbers: ICLmath 75.7 GSM8K / 36.8 MATH (avg 56.3); ICLbio 77.9 / 34.9 (avg 56.4); relevant 71.5 / 33.3 (avg 52.4); N/A 75.5 / 36.1 (avg 55.8). Gain of fixed verified examples over relevant: about 4 points average.
limits: GPT-3.5 only in the main table. No direct token count against self-consistency in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Cheaper and safer: keep a small verified exemplar bank instead of asking the model to invent analogs per query. Compare with self-consistency before adopting analogical prompting.

source: Lin, Pan, Li et al. (2025) MetaLadder: Ascending Mathematical Solution Quality via Analogical-Problem Reasoning Transfer
finding: Gap 8. Trains models on data that contains an analogous meta-problem with its solution and a problem restatement before the target. Gains over CoT-trained models. It is fine-tuning, not a prompt-only scaffold.
numbers: Llama3-8B +6.7 points average (36.1 to 42.8) and DeepSeekMath-7B +10.3 points (47.3 to 57.6) over CoT training; +5.4 and +9.5 over RefAug. Inference time: GSM8K Llama CoT 61.9 s vs MetaLadder 172.6 s; MATH 749 s vs 1480 s; DeepSeek 65.9 s vs 210.2 s and 1253 s vs 2181 s. A shortcut variant cuts this to about 111 to 114 s on GSM8K.
limits: Training-time method; analog problems were produced and solved by a strong model during data annotation. Not comparable to a zero-training scaffold. No self-consistency baseline at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Small models can use analogous solved problems when taught to, at 1.7x to 3x inference time. For a scaffold without training, the analogous problem would have to be retrieved or verified.

source: Inani, Kabra, Marupudi, Varma (2025) Modeling Understanding of Story-Based Analogies Using Large Language Models (CogSci 2025)
finding: Gap 7. On the 18 Gentner-style stories from Webb 2023, modern LLMs reach human-level accuracy but do not track which items are hard for people. Sentence-embedding similarity alone gets 78% but has no item-level link to humans. A prompt in which the model first writes its own explanation raises accuracy but lowers human-likeness.
numbers: Embedding accuracy 0.78 vs human 0.847 (GPT-3 0.75); item-level correlation of embedding margin with human item accuracy r = -0.032, p = .899. Conventional-prompt accuracy: GPT-4o-mini 0.7011, GPT-4o 0.8233, Llama-3.1-8B 0.6528, Llama-3.1-70B 0.8538; enhanced (explain-first) prompts up to 0.9150. Larger models at least 15% better than small. Only GPT-4o-mini with the conventional prompt correlated with human item difficulty (r = 0.526, p = 0.025).
limits: Only 18 items; 100 runs per model. Table columns in the PDF text are scrambled, so which enhanced-prompt number belongs to which model is uncertain; the maximum 0.9150 and the Llama-70B 0.8538 are the sure ones.
agent_relevance: Surface similarity (embeddings) already gives 78% on this benchmark, so about 80-85% accuracy can be had without mapping. Use harder, overlap-controlled items.

source: Lee, Song, Yoon, Park, Kang (2025) The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Gap 9 and 7. Interpretability on proportional and story analogies in open models. Relational information is present in mid-upper layers when the answer is right; failures come from missing relation info or from failing to apply it to the new entity. Successful story analogies show higher structural alignment between source and target; failures show alignment to the distractor.
numbers: Patching hidden states at key positions fixed up to 38.4% of failed proportional cases by replacing the first pair, and up to 38.1% by patching relation information (Gemma-7B row), up to 61.9% in a third setting. Models include Llama-2-13B, Gemma-7B, Qwen2.5-14B. A probe reached 82.9% for one analogy distinction.
limits: Open models of 7B to 14B only. I read the abstract, the patching table and the alignment section, not the full method. Correlation of alignment with success is not proof of mechanism. The meaning of the third column (61.9%) was not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Application of a known relation is a separate failure point from extracting it. A scaffold step that states the relation in plain words, then applies it to the target entity, covers both.

source: Opielka, Rosenbusch, Stevenson (2025) Analogical Reasoning Inside Large Language Models: Concept Vectors and the Limits of Abstraction
finding: Gap 9. Function vectors are not invariant to simple input changes. A few attention heads hold invariant concept vectors for verbal concepts such as antonym, but none for abstract concepts like previous/next, which are tied to known ordered lists. Letter-string accuracy of Llama-3.1 70B falls as the alphabet is permuted.
numbers: Llama-3.1 70B letter-string accuracy by number of permuted letters: 0 -> 0.35, 2 -> 0.10, 5 -> 0.05, 10 -> 0.00, 20 -> 0.00, symbol alphabet 0.15 (chance 0.04 letters, 0.10 symbols). Mean concept-vector similarity 0.8 for same concept, 0.7 across languages; abstract-letter 'next' 0.16 against 0.75 for verbal concepts. Patching a concept vector changed behaviour causally.
limits: Open model, linear-representation assumption, small prompt sets. Only 'next' analysed for the letter task because 'previous' was near zero.
agent_relevance: Abstract relations tied to familiar lists do not generalise inside the model, so forcing the relation into explicit words, or renaming objects, may help. Not tested directly.

source: Camposampiero, Hersche, Wattenhofer, Sebastian, Rahimi (2025) Can Large Reasoning Models do Analogical Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty?
finding: Gap 1 and 3. Reasoning models (o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1) solve Raven-type matrices well on the clean set but collapse when rule length, value range and noise grow, despite 3.4x more reasoning tokens. A neuro-symbolic abductive model stays robust.
numbers: o3-mini 86.6% on I-RAVEN to 17.0% on I-RAVEN-X with uncertainty (chance 12.5%); DeepSeek-R1 80.6% to 23.2%. High reasoning effort lifted o3-mini only to 31.0% at an average of 53,596 reasoning tokens. Neuro-symbolic ARLC 98.6% to 88.0%. Plain LLMs fall to near 0% arithmetic accuracy on the larger ranges.
limits: Raven-type symbolic attribute matrices, not letter strings or ConceptARC. Two models, a 2025 snapshot.
agent_relevance: Long chain of thought is not enough once the number of values to bind grows; fits a capacity story and favours chunked or tool-assisted processing, but no chunking arm was run (Gap 3 stays open).

source: Cheng Jiayang, Qiu, Chan et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: Deriving Story-level Analogies from Large Language Models
finding: Gap 7. A 24K story-pair corpus with human labels of entity and relational similarity from extended structure-mapping theory. Identifying analogies is hard for embeddings and LLMs.
numbers: ChatGPT about 30% accuracy on analogy identification versus over 85% for humans (abstract text). Story-pairs 24K.
limits: I read the abstract, introduction and start of the results table; I did not re-check the 30% in a table cell. Task format (identify among candidates) differs from Webb's two-choice items, so numbers are not comparable to the 2023 GPT-4 results.
agent_relevance: Near-ceiling results on two-choice story items depend on item design. When the benchmark requires identifying analogs among many stories, models fall to about 30%.

source: Xiang, Ma, Cao, Zhu, Zhu (2026) Grounding Before Generalizing: How AI Differs from Humans in Causal Transfer
finding: Gap 4 (indirect). In an interactive causal-structure task, models need to relearn the new environment before showing transfer, whereas humans use the structure from the first attempt. Text-only models matched or beat human discovery efficiency, but vision input made them worse.
numbers: 30 agents per model per structure. Humans 65.0% success on both Common Cause and Common Effect, 19.4 and 22.0 attempts. Models 66.7% to 100% depending on model and condition. GPT 5.2 text: 100.0% on CC vs 66.7% on CE with 19.7 attempts on CE.
limits: Interactive exploration task, not a retrieval test. No explicit analog memory in the setup. Transfer ratios not extracted.
agent_relevance: No direct evidence on retrieval versus mapping. Transfer of learned structure to a new surface is slow in models; a scaffold note of the structure learned so far may help (untested).

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical Mapping by Constraint Satisfaction, Tables 5 and 15 re-read from the scanned text
finding: Gap 10. Table 15 (jealous-animal stories, ACME): cycles to success 3, 4 and 38 for systematic S/S, D, S/D; non-systematic 3, 4 and no success in the cross-mapped S/D version. Table 5 (four lightbulb/radiation versions): the text says ACME maps all four, cycles do not depend on surface similarity and rise slightly for the two poor-constraint versions. Human data of Holyoak and Koh 1987 read as 69%, 33%, 13% before the hint and 75%, 60%, 47% with the hint, but the scan puts a 38 and an 81 in the wrong cells.
numbers: Table 15: systematic 3 / 4 / 38 cycles; unsystematic 3 / 4 / no success. Default inhibition -.2, min -1; success restored by inhibition -.1 or min -.3. Table 5: cycles 3 and 5 are certain for the first and last columns; the 38 in the second column is a bleed from Table 15. Human percentages 69, 33, 13 (before hint), 75, 60, 47 (with hint); one value (81) unassigned.
quote: cycles to success does not differ as a function of surface similarity
limits: OCR of a 1989 scan; assignment of Table 5 numbers to columns is inferred from the text. Check the original print (Cognitive Science 13) before quoting by condition. The source was opened from a local text copy made earlier (ht89.txt), re-read this session.
agent_relevance: ACME's one weakness is cross-mapped unsystematic stories under default parameters; a scaffold that scores structural and semantic evidence should expose that trade-off.
